passage:
Diary, Tuesday.
Big fight with Lavanya today. It's her bat, so she always bats first and longest, and everyone lets her. I was so angry I almost went to tell Sir. Then I thought he'd just take the bat away and nobody would play. So I said, "Your bat, fine, but everyone gets six balls, then switch." She said, "No, Wasim." I said, "Then I'll bring my tennis ball tomorrow and we'll use a plank." She laughed, but then agreed to six balls. Half the group cheered. I think it'll work. 🤞

qa.q: How many balls did Wasim suggest each player gets?
qa.a: Six balls, then switch.

qa.q: Why did Wasim decide not to tell Sir?
qa.a: Wasim worried Sir would just take the bat away and then nobody would get to play.

qa.q: What made Wasim's approach work?
qa.a: Wasim offered a fair rule that still let Lavanya keep her bat, and gave a calm alternative instead of just shouting.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see the new rule?
qa.a: She loses some batting time but keeps everyone playing with her bat, and her laugh suggests she didn't feel attacked.

grounding: It shows a child handling a power imbalance in a game by negotiating a fair rule without going to an adult.

passage: Behind the village school there was one rope swing on the banyan, and Tushar, the tallest boy in Class 5, had held it all break for three days. Lavanya, ten, marched up. "You don't own it." "I got here first." The other children watched, waiting to see who would run for Masterji. Lavanya didn't. She picked up a stick and scratched a line in the dust. "Twenty pushes each, then the next one in line. I'll count for you first." Tushar hesitated, looking at the line of faces. Then he shrugged. "Fine. But count fair." She did.

qa.q: What did Lavanya scratch in the dust?
qa.a: She scratched a line in the dust with a stick.

qa.q: Why did Tushar hesitate before agreeing?
qa.a: He probably didn't want to lose his hold on the swing, but he also noticed everyone watching and didn't want to look unfair.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's plan get right?
qa.a: It set a clear, equal rule and began with Tushar's turn, so he could agree without losing face.

qa.q: How might the watching children see the outcome?
qa.a: They get a fair turn at last and see a problem sorted out without an adult stepping in.

grounding: It shows a village girl settling a dispute with a stronger peer herself rather than fetching the teacher.

passage: In a classroom in Lisbon, Kwame and Ines were stuck on their volcano poster. Ines had grabbed the markers and was writing every heading herself. "You always take over," Kwame said, louder than he meant. Ines snapped, "Because you're slow." Two tables away, the teacher looked up. Kwame took a breath. "Okay. What if you write and I draw? You're faster at writing, and I'm better at the diagram." Ines stared at the half-empty poster, then slid the black marker over. "Fine. But the lava has to be orange." By the end of the lesson they were arguing only about shades of orange.

qa.q: What were Kwame and Ines making?
qa.a: A volcano poster.

qa.q: What was Kwame feeling when he said "You always take over"?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and pushed aside because Ines had grabbed all the markers.

qa.q: What helped the argument cool down?
qa.a: Kwame took a breath and suggested splitting the work by strengths, which gave both of them a real role.

qa.q: What would change if the teacher had come over at once?
qa.a: She might have assigned the jobs herself, and the two would have missed working it out on their own.

grounding: It shows two classmates resolving a power struggle over a shared task without the teacher stepping in.

passage: At the cricket nets of the sports club, Vaibhav, the tallest in the under-12 group, announced he'd bat first, second and third. Rafiq crossed his arms. 'That's not fair. You batted first yesterday too.' The coach was busy with the seniors. Vaibhav scowled. 'I'm the best batsman.' Rafiq didn't back down. 'Then prove it in turns. Six balls each, and we write the order on the board.' Some others nodded. Vaibhav kicked the pad, then picked up the chalk. 'Fine. But I'm writing.' He put himself third.

qa.q: Where was the coach during the argument?
qa.a: The coach was busy with the seniors.

qa.q: What might Rafiq have been feeling when he crossed his arms?
qa.a: He felt that Vaibhav's claim was unfair and was determined to stand up to him.

qa.q: What worked in how the boys solved it without the coach?
qa.a: Rafiq proposed a clear, fair rule and others backed him, which balanced Vaibhav's power.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see putting himself third?
qa.a: He may feel he lost some control but saved face by holding the chalk and writing the order himself.

grounding: Illustrates children settling a power struggle among peers with little adult help, at a sports club.

passage: I sit behind Ramesh and Gautam in Class 7, so I saw the whole thing. For the science model, both wanted to be the leader. Ramesh said his idea was better; Gautam said Ramesh always bosses. They didn't talk for two periods. Then at lunch I saw Gautam push a paper across: two columns, 'your jobs', 'my jobs'. Ramesh read it, crossed out one line and wrote something. Gautam shrugged and nodded. After that, they were whispering about batteries. I don't know who won, but nobody told the teacher.

qa.q: What did Gautam push across at lunch?
qa.a: A paper with two columns: 'your jobs' and 'my jobs'.

qa.q: What might Gautam have felt when saying Ramesh always bosses?
qa.a: Gautam likely felt frustrated and pushed around, and wanted a fair share of control.

qa.q: How could the boys handle a similar clash next time?
qa.a: They could start by splitting jobs on paper right away, since that helped them settle it.

qa.q: How does the narrator see the conflict?
qa.a: The narrator watches with interest and notices the boys solved it themselves, but isn't sure who 'won'.

grounding: Shows two children resolving a power struggle over leadership without adult intervention, seen by a classmate.

passage: Week one: Hemant, nine, and Irawati fought over the colony cricket bat. Hemant grabbed it; Irawati ran to tell the watchman uncle, who made them share. Week two: they argued again. This time Hemant said, "Five overs each, then swap." Irawati said, "Six for me, I'm bowling first." They shouted a bit, then agreed. Week four: both wanted to bat first. Nobody went to the watchman. Irawati flipped a coin. Hemant lost, groaned, and picked up the ball.

qa.q: What did Irawati do in week one?
qa.a: She ran to tell the watchman uncle.

qa.q: What does Hemant groaning but picking up the ball suggest?
qa.a: He felt disappointed, but accepted the fair coin toss without needing an adult.

qa.q: What helped them solve arguments on their own?
qa.a: Making simple rules together, like turns and a coin toss, so they didn't need the watchman.

qa.q: How might the watchman see the change by week four?
qa.a: He would probably be relieved and pleased that they sorted it out themselves.

grounding: Shows two children moving over a month from needing an adult to settle fights to resolving them alone.

passage: "When I, your Leela Paati, was ten, our street had one big mango tree, and the boys said it was theirs. Tanvir was their leader. One summer he pushed me off the lowest branch. I wanted to run to my father, but I thought, then Appa will shout, and Tanvir will hate me more. So I went back the next day with a chalk line and said, 'Mornings for us, afternoons for you.' He laughed. I didn't move. After a week of arguing, he agreed. We shared that tree for years, and later he was the one who taught me to climb higher."

qa.q: What did Leela bring back the next day?
qa.a: A chalk line.

qa.q: What was Leela thinking when she decided not to run to her father?
qa.a: She was worried that her father's shouting would make Tanvir resent her more, so she wanted to solve it herself.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the deal possible?
qa.a: Leela coming back with a clear offer and not moving when Tanvir laughed.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have seen Leela after that week?
qa.a: He probably began to respect her, which is why he later taught her to climb.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child she negotiated with a stronger peer herself instead of calling an adult.

passage: The group project was due tomorrow, and the power was out. Sumit, eleven, and Gurpreet sat on her verandah with a torch and a chart. "I'll present," said Sumit. "You always present," said Gurpreet. "I made the drawings." They glared. Sumit thought of calling their teacher, but it was nine at night. "Okay," he said, "you do the first half, I do the second." Gurpreet frowned. "And we practise now, in the torchlight." They did, twice, and she laughed when he forgot his lines.

qa.q: What were Sumit and Gurpreet working on?
qa.a: A group project chart.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet glare at Sumit?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair that he always presented, even though she made the drawings.

qa.q: Which choice resolved the argument, and why?
qa.a: Splitting the presentation in half, because it shared the credit fairly without an adult.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel when Gurpreet laughs at his forgotten lines?
qa.a: Probably a bit embarrassed but relieved, since her laughter shows the argument is over.

grounding: Shows two children settling a power struggle over a project on their own, under time pressure and a power cut.

passage: The shuttle landed right on the line of the Andheri society's badminton court. "Out!" Himani shouted. "In!" Nandini shouted back. Himani was twelve and always decided things. "I'm older, so it's out." Nandini's cheeks burned. Last year she would have run upstairs to get Mummy. Instead she took a breath. "We both can't see it properly from here. Let's replay the point." Himani frowned, spinning her racquet. "Fine. But I serve." "Fine," Nandini said. They replayed it. Himani won the point, but Nandini didn't mind as much.

qa.q: How old was Himani?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt angry and frustrated that Himani used being older to decide the point.

qa.q: What worked in how Nandini handled the argument?
qa.a: She stayed calm and suggested a fair replay instead of fighting or running for an adult.

qa.q: How might Himani see Nandini's suggestion?
qa.a: Himani might feel slightly challenged but agree because the replay was fair.

grounding: A girl resolves a badminton dispute with an older, bossy neighbour by suggesting a replay, without fetching a parent.

passage:
"I should present. I did the drawings," said Gurleen.
"But I wrote all the facts," Chaitanya said. "You'll get them wrong."
"I won't!"
"You will. Remember the volcano one?"
Gurleen crossed her arms. "Fine, let's ask Ma'am."
Chaitanya stopped. "She'll just choose for us. Then we both might lose."
"So what, then?"
"You show the drawings and I say the facts. Half-half."
"And who starts?"
"Coin toss."
Gurleen uncrossed her arms. "Deal. But if you say 'um' more than three times, I take over."
"Deal," Chaitanya laughed.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do for the project?
qa.a: The drawings.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and defensive after Chaitanya said she would get the facts wrong.

qa.q: Which choice helped them settle it without the teacher?
qa.a: Splitting the talk half-half and using a coin toss to decide who starts.

qa.q: What would change if they had asked Ma'am to choose?
qa.a: The teacher might have picked one of them, leaving the other upset and the quarrel unsolved between them.

grounding: Two children settle a presentation argument by sharing the parts themselves instead of asking the teacher.

passage: I'm Sudha. Last year, whenever Kiran grabbed the swing at recess, I ran straight to the teacher. The teacher would sigh and make one of us wait. We both ended up sulking. This year, when Kiran got on the swing first again, I nearly went, then stopped. I said, "Let's count to fifty each and swap." Kiran rolled her eyes but agreed. The first time she tried to count really slowly, and I called it out. We laughed. Now we don't even need to count out loud. I still think about how much easier it is when we sort it out ourselves.

qa.q: What did Sudha suggest instead of going to the teacher?
qa.a: Counting to fifty each and then swapping.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after sorting things out with Kiran?
qa.a: Sudha felt pleased and relieved that it was easier when they solved it themselves.

qa.q: What could Sudha do if Kiran broke the counting rule again?
qa.a: Sudha could call it out calmly again, as before, and suggest a fair fix together.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the new counting rule?
qa.a: Kiran may have been a little annoyed at first but seems to find it fair, and even funny.

grounding: A child looks back on moving from running to the teacher to settling swing turns with a friend directly.

passage:
Games teacher's note, Friday.

This week, Zeenat and three friends argued every day about who would be football captain. On Monday it ended in tears and I stepped in.

On Wednesday, I decided to wait. They shouted for a while. Then Zeenat said, "What if we take turns? One day each." Pooja said, "But I go first." Zeenat said, "Fine, but then me."

They made a list on the wall. Today, nobody came to me. I'll keep standing back.

— Naveen

qa.q: What did Zeenat suggest?
qa.a: Zeenat said, "What if we take turns? One day each."

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when the arguing stopped?
qa.a: Zeenat probably felt relieved and proud that the idea worked.

qa.q: How did Naveen support the children's conflict resolution?
qa.a: Naveen stepped back and let them solve it themselves, only watching.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel going first?
qa.a: Pooja likely felt happy and satisfied at getting the first turn.

grounding: A games teacher notes children resolving a captaincy argument themselves, with less adult help.

passage:
Durga Puja holidays, Saturday

Big fight with Ishita today. We were practising the dance for the building function, and she said I was always in the front. I said she never learns the steps.

She went home. I sat on the stairs for ages, still angry. Then I thought, she's right, I did take the front every time.

So I went to her flat. I said, "Sorry for saying you don't learn the steps. You can have the front on the first night."

She said, "And you can have it on the second."

We practised for another hour. Ma didn't even know we had fought.

Ganga

qa.q: What did Ishita say about the dance?
qa.a: She said Ganga was always in the front.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel sitting on the stairs?
qa.a: Ganga felt angry at first, then guilty on realising Ishita was right.

qa.q: What helped Ganga and Ishita solve the fight without an adult?
qa.a: Ganga thought about her own part, apologised, and offered a fair turn at the front.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Ganga came to apologise?
qa.a: Ishita was likely relieved and willing to make up.

grounding: During Durga Puja holidays, a child resolves a fight with a friend over who dances in front without adult help.

passage:
During Makar Sankranti in the village near Solapur, Zeenat, eleven, and Ankita, nine, were flying kites on the roof.

Zeenat, the older one, took Ankita's best kite. "I'll fly it better."

Ankita crossed her arms. "It's mine. You always take things because you're bigger."

Zeenat stopped. Nobody had ever said that to her.

"Okay," she said. "You fly it, and I'll hold the spool."

Ankita was surprised. They flew it together, and it went higher than any other kite on the street.

qa.q: Who held the spool?
qa.a: Zeenat held the spool.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when Ankita said she always takes things?
qa.a: Zeenat felt surprised and a bit ashamed, since nobody had said it to her before.

qa.q: What helped the girls resolve the argument without adults?
qa.a: Ankita spoke up clearly, and Zeenat listened and offered to share the job.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Zeenat agreed?
qa.a: Ankita was surprised and likely happy to be listened to.

grounding: During Sankranti, two girls in a village resolve a kite argument and an older child's power imbalance on their own.

passage: The first real snow had fallen in Tromsø, and the slope behind the school was packed at break. Anders, the biggest boy in fifth grade, had taken the best sledge and was deciding who got a go. "Not you, Emil. You're too slow." Emil's face went hot. He almost ran to the teacher on duty, then stopped. Instead he gathered the others. "Let's go in order of who got here first. Everyone gets two runs." Most of them nodded. Anders scowled, outnumbered. "Fine. But I go first." "You were first anyway," Emil said. By the bell, Anders was pushing the little ones off from the top himself.

qa.q: How many runs did Emil suggest each person get?
qa.a: Everyone gets two runs.

qa.q: Why did Emil stop himself from running to the teacher on duty?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, but seemed confident the group could agree on a fair rule without help.

qa.q: What made Emil's plan work?
qa.a: He offered a simple, fair rule and got the others to agree first, so Anders couldn't just overrule him. 👍

qa.q: What is it like for Anders when the others nod at Emil's plan?
qa.a: Anders feels outnumbered and a bit put out, but accepts because Emil lets him save face by going first.

grounding: Shows children settling a power struggle over a sledge among themselves instead of calling an adult.
